```{r}
#| label: load dataset
#| echo: FALSE

survdat   <- readRDS("./survival_workshop_data.rds")
constants <- survdat$constants
raw       <- survdat$raw
```

```{r}
#| label: create data frame
#| echo: FALSE

# same derivation as Parts 1 and 2
analysis <- raw |>
  mutate(
    time   = as.numeric(date_last_contact - date_considered) / constants$days_per_month,
    status = as.integer(outcome == "Relapsed")
  ) |>
  arrange(date_considered)

analysis <- analysis |>
  mutate(group = relevel(factor(group), ref = "placebo"),
         stage = factor(stage, levels = c("I", "II", "III")))
```

## Where we left off

- Kaplan-Meier **describes** survival
- The log-rank test **compares** survival curves
- Neither tells us about the effect of our dependent variables:
  - **By how much** do the groups differ?
  - What if patients also differ in age, stage, biomarker...?

::: notes
In the previous lecture we looked at Kaplan-Meier (KM) curves. We discussed
that these curves *describe* a survival curve (the probability of surviving
past time $t$ given that you have survived up to that point). The log-rank 
test 
:::

## From survival to hazard

- **Survival** $S(t)$: probability of being event-free past time $t$
- **Instantaneous hazard** $h(t)$: the risk of the event at $t$, **given** 
you've made it to $t$
- **Cumulative hazard** $H(t)$: the cumulative probability of subjects
experiencing the event up to a give time $t$


## Instantaneous to cumulative hazard

$$
\begin{aligned}
h(t) &= \frac{\text{rate at which survival declines}}{\text{proportion still surviving}}
      = -\frac{S'(t)}{S(t)}
      = -\frac{d}{dt}\log S(t) \\[6pt]
H(t) &= \int_0^{t} h(u)\,du = -\log S(t) \\[6pt]
S(t) &= e^{-H(t)}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Calculating cumulative hazard

```{r}
#| label: cumulative hazard by group
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

km_group  <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ group, data = analysis)
cumhaz_df <- km_df(km_group) |>
  mutate(cumhaz = -log(surv)) |>
  filter(is.finite(cumhaz))

ggplot(cumhaz_df, aes(time, cumhaz, colour = strata)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#d6604d", "#4393c3")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, max(analysis$time))) +
  labs(x = "Months since study entry",
       y = "Cumulative hazard  H(t) = −log S(t)",
       colour = NULL,
       title = "Risk accumulated over follow-up",
       subtitle = "Slope (derivative) at any point is the instantaneous hazard") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

::: notes

hazard. Survival goes down as hazard accumulates.
:::

## What "proportional" means

$$h(t \mid x) = h_0(t)\, e^{\beta x}$$
- $h(t \mid x)$ the instantaneous hazard at time $t$ given some covariates $x$
product of:
  - $h_0(t)$: the **baseline hazard**, the hazard when $x = 0$ (the reference
  group) AND
  - $e^{\beta x}$: how much the covariates $x$ multiply the baseline $h_0(t)$
- curves can have any shape
  - upshot: one is always a fixed multiple of the other and so are
  *proportional*

## How Cox fits the model: risk sets again

- At each event time: of everyone **at risk**, how likely was it that
*this* person had the event, given their covariates?
- Multiply over event times the **partial likelihood**
- $h_0(t)$ cancels out, which is why we never have to specify it

$$
\begin{aligned}
L_i(\beta) &= \frac{h_0(t_i)\, e^{\beta x_i}}{\sum_{j \in R(t_i)} h_0(t_i)\, e^{\beta x_j}}
            = \frac{e^{\beta x_i}}{\sum_{j \in R(t_i)} e^{\beta x_j}} \\[8pt]
\end{aligned}
$$

::: notes
When working with Cox-PH models we never estimate the baseline hazard $h_0$
directly; instead, we calculate the partial likelihood ($\mathcal{L}_i(\beta)$).
This is simply the relative probability of an individual $i$ with given
covariates $x_i$ of experiencing the event at time $t$. NOtice that this is just
the ratio between the multiplier $e^{\beta x_i}$ and the others in the risk 
set.
:::

## One covariate: treatment group

```{r}
#| label: cox group
cox_group <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ group, data = analysis)
summary(cox_group)
```

::: notes
Now that we've touched on the background material needed to understand CoxPH
models let's actually start looking at (and interpreting) some output. First,
the `coef`. This is on the scale and is 
log($\frac{h_{\text{maintenance}}}{h_{\text{placebo}}}$). It can be interpreted
as showing that our intervention (maintenance) decreased the risk of 
experiencing the event (given the negative sign of the coefficient), but not 
too much more than than that (easily anyway). To get a real sense of how much
our intervention affected the probability of relapse, we can look one output 
to the right `exp(coef)`. This is the exponentiated version of the hazard 
ratio seen to the left. Recall that the null hypothesis for this statistical
test predicts that there should be no effect of the treatment (maintenance) 
on the hazard so the ratio $\frac{h_{\text{maintenance}}}{h_{\text{placebo}}}$
is 1 by our null hypothesis. So,
$\frac{h_{\text{maintenance}}}{h_{\text{placebo}}} < 1$ implies that our
treatment decreased the hazard. To see by how much we need subtract this ratio
from 1 which leads to a 46% reduction in the hazard (or instantaneous rate) of
relapse.
:::

## Log-rank reloaded

```{r}
#| label: score vs log-rank
summary(cox_group)$sctest                                     # Cox score test
survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ group, data = analysis)$chisq   # Part 2 log-rank
```

::: notes
The Cox model reproduces the log-rank test, then adds what it couldn't give us:
an effect size.
:::

## Hazard ratios `r emoji::emoji('not')` survival probabilities

- HR = 0.6 does **not** mean 40% fewer people relapse
  - instead: a 40% lower **rate** at every moment in risk set
- survival probabilities: go back to $S(t)$

```{r}
#| label: hr vs survival
#| eval: false

nd <- data.frame(group = levels(analysis$group))
summary(survfit(cox_group, newdata = nd), times = 24)
```

::: notes
Show the HR next to the 24-month survival in each group. Probability of
surviving past month 24 is 79% for the placebo and 88% for the maintenance 
group (about 9% difference).
:::

## Continuous covariates: age

```{r}
#| label: cox age
#| eval: false

# HR per 10 years
# I() = 'Inhibit Interpretation'
# I(age / 10) creates a new column age/10
# without I() R would try to 'group' age by 10 which would not make sense
# so each per-unit (1) increase in age actually correponds to 10 years :)
cox_age <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ I(age / 10), data = analysis) 
summary(cox_age)
```

::: notes
The model assumes each extra 10 years multiplies the hazard by the
same amount (log-linear). Now that we've touched on the background material
needed to understand CoxPH models let's actually start looking at (and
interpreting) some output. First, the `coef`. This is on the scale and is 
log($\frac{h_{\text{age} + 10}}{h_{\text{age}}}$). It can be interpreted
as showing that our age increased the risk of 
experiencing the event (given the positive sign of the coefficient), but not 
too much more than than that (easily anyway). To get a real sense of how much
our intervention affected the probability of relapse, we can look one output 
to the right `exp(coef)`. This is the exponentiated version of the hazard 
ratio seen to the left. Recall that the null hypothesis for this statistical
test predicts that there should be no effect of the treatment (maintenance) 
on the hazard so the ratio log($\frac{h_{\text{age} + 10}}{h_{\text{age}}}$)
is 1 by our null hypothesis. So,
$\frac{h_{\text{age} + 10}}{h_{\text{age}}} < 1$ implies that our
age increased the hazard. To see by how much we need subtract this ratio
from 1 which leads to a 7% increase in the hazard (or instantaneous rate) of
relapse per 10 years increase of age. However, our p-value is highly
insignificant at `p = 0.302`, so we cannot definitely say that age affects
relapse time (or it at least does not do so log-linearly).
:::

## Add the biomarker covariate

```{r}
#| label: cox ph with biomarker
#| eval: false

# Note that: log_2(2x) = log_2(x) + 1 (a one-unit increase on the log2 scale)
# This model asks how the hazard changes when the biomarker doubles:
# HR = h(2 * biomarker) / h(biomarker)
cox_bio <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ log2(biomarker), data = analysis) 
summary(cox_bio)
```

::: notes
The model assumes each extra 10 years multiplies the hazard by the
same amount (log-linear). Now that we've touched on the background material
needed to understand CoxPH models let's actually start looking at (and
interpreting) some output. First, the `coef`. This is on the scale and is 
log($\frac{h_{\text{biomarker} * 2}}{h_{\text{biomarker}}}$). It can be interpreted
as showing that our age increased the risk of 
experiencing the event (given the positive sign of the coefficient), but not 
too much more than than that (easily anyway). To get a real sense of how much
our intervention affected the probability of relapse, we can look one output 
to the right `exp(coef)`. This is the exponentiated version of the hazard 
ratio seen to the left. Recall that the null hypothesis for this statistical
test predicts that there should be no effect of the treatment (maintenance) 
on the hazard so the ratio 
log($\frac{h_{\text{biomarker} * 2}}{h_{\text{biomarker}}}$)
is 1 by our null hypothesis. So,
$\log(\frac{h_{\text{biomarker} * 2}}{h_{\text{biomarker}}}) < 1$ implies that
our age increased the hazard. To see by how much we need subtract this ratio
from 1 which leads to a 7% increase in the hazard (or instantaneous rate) of
relapse per 10 years increase of age. However, our p-value is highly
significant, so we can definitely say that biomarker affects
relapse time.
:::

## The multivariable model

```{r}
#| label: cox full
#| eval: false

cox_full <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ group + I(age / 10) + sex + stage + log2(biomarker),
                  data = analysis)
summary(cox_full)
```

- Each HR is **adjusted** for every other covariate in the model
- TODO: compare the treatment HR with and without adjustment

::: notes
Now we are looking at the full multivariable model, which evaluates each
predictor while holding all other variables constant (`n = 513`, `212` events). 

* **Treatment (`groupmaintenance`):** After adjusting for age, sex, 
disease stage, and biomarker levels, maintenance therapy still shows a strong 
protective effect—cutting the relapse hazard by about **52%** (`HR = 0.48`,
`p < 0.001`), which is even stronger than the 46% reduction we saw in the
unadjusted model.

* **Age (`I(age/10)`):** Each 10-year increase in age is associated with
roughly a **9% higher hazard** (`HR = 1.09`), but this remains statistically
non-significant (`p = 0.22`).
* **Sex (`sexMale`):** Compared to the reference group (Female), males
have a **32% higher hazard** of relapse (`HR = 1.32`, `p = 0.046`).
* **Disease Stage (`stageII` & `stageIII`):** Compared to Stage I (the
reference group), Stage II patients have a **45% higher hazard** (`HR = 1.45`,
`p = 0.018`), while Stage III patients face more than 
**2.6 times the hazard** (`HR = 2.61`, `p < 0.001`).
* **Biomarker (`log2(biomarker)`):** Every **doubling** of the biomarker
increases the relapse hazard by about **31%** (`HR = 1.31`, `p = 0.0015`).

Treatment group, disease stage, and baseline biomarker levels are our
strongest independent predictors of relapse time.
:::

## Plot survival curves

```{r}
#| label: predicted curves
#| eval: false

nd <- data.frame(group = c("placebo", "maintenance"),
                 age = 60,
                 sex = "Female",
                 stage = "II",
                 biomarker = median(analysis$biomarker))
fit_adj <- survfit(cox_full, newdata = nd)
plot(fit_adj, col = c("#E64B35", "#4DBBD5"), lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Time", ylab = "Relapse-Free Survival Probability")
legend("bottomleft", legend = c("Placebo", "Maintenance"),
       col = c("#E64B35", "#4DBBD5"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

::: notes
These are adjusted survival curves for a specific type of patient 
(a 60-year-old female with Stage II disease and median biomarker levels), 
rather than a raw population average—isolating the treatment effect while
accounting for confounding variables (e.g., disease-stage) that we are 
interested in accounting for but not necessarily making inference on.
:::

## What we assumed

- The hazard ratio is the **same at every point in follow-up**
- Continuous covariates act **log-linearly** on the hazard
- Censoring is **non-informative** (same as Parts 1–2)

## Summary

- The **hazard** is the instantaneous risk of the event among those still at
risk
- Cox: $h(t \mid x) = h_0(t)\, e^{\beta x}$, with the baseline hazard left
unspecified (semi-parametric)
- Fitted from the same risk sets as KM and the log-rank test
- Output: **hazard ratios**, adjusted for the other covariates
- HRs are **not** survival probabilities
